q: Explain the Neutron architecture: server, ML2 plugin, agents and mechanism drivers.
a: Neutron is the networking service. The neutron-server exposes the API and stores networks, subnets, ports and routers in the database. It uses the ML2 plugin, a modular framework with type drivers, which define how a network is built, such as flat, vlan, vxlan or geneve, and mechanism drivers, which actually program the back end, such as Open vSwitch, Linux bridge or OVN. In the classic OVS design, agents run on every node: the OVS agent wires ports, the DHCP agent runs dnsmasq per network, the L3 agent runs routers in namespaces, and the metadata agent proxies instance metadata. In the OVN design most of that logic moves into the OVN databases and ovn-controller on each host. I explain it as control plane in neutron-server and a data plane implemented by whichever mechanism driver you choose.
f: What does a type driver do versus a mechanism driver?
Which agents disappear with OVN?
p: neutron-server holds the API and DB; ML2 combines type drivers (flat, vlan, vxlan, geneve) with mechanism drivers (OVS, OVN, Linux bridge) that program the data plane; agents run per node.
tip: Separate control plane (server and DB) from data plane (driver) in the answer.

q: OVS versus OVN: what changed and why do most new clouds choose OVN?
a: ML2 with Open vSwitch uses a set of Python agents on every node: the OVS agent, L3 agent, DHCP agent and metadata agent, communicating over RabbitMQ, and routers run as Linux namespaces, which adds control-plane chatter and scale limits. OVN, Open Virtual Network, moves logical networking into a dedicated database model. Neutron writes logical switches, routers, ACLs and ports to the OVN northbound database, ovn-northd translates them into logical flows in the southbound database, and ovn-controller on each hypervisor programs OVS locally. Routing and security groups become OpenFlow rules distributed on every host, so DVR style east-west routing is built in, DHCP and metadata are handled by ovn-controller, and RabbitMQ load drops. The benefits are better scale, simpler operations and fewer moving parts, which is why new clouds default to OVN.
f: What are the northbound and southbound databases?
How do you migrate from OVS to OVN?
p: OVN replaces the agent-based design with logical networking in OVN databases, ovn-northd translation and ovn-controller on each host. Fewer agents, less RabbitMQ chatter, distributed routing by default.
tip: Name northd and ovn-controller to show you know the pipeline.

q: What is the difference between provider networks and tenant (self-service) networks?
a: Provider networks map directly onto physical networks that the operator defined, typically flat or VLAN, and instances attach to them like machines on the data-centre network. They are created by admins, have real routable addresses, and use the external router, so performance is simple and predictable, and they are common for production and for telco. Tenant networks, also called self-service, are created by users inside their project, usually as VXLAN or Geneve overlays, and are connected to external networks by a virtual router with SNAT and floating IPs. They give isolation and self-service, overlapping address ranges between tenants, and no involvement from the network team, at the cost of encapsulation overhead and a more complex data path. Many clouds use both: tenant networks for general workloads and provider networks for workloads that need direct addressing.
f: Why can tenants overlap IP ranges?
When would you offer provider networks to tenants?
p: Provider networks are operator-defined mappings to physical VLANs with routable addresses. Tenant networks are user-created overlays routed to the outside through a virtual router and floating IPs.
cmds: openstack network create --provider-network-type vlan --provider-physical-network physnet1 --provider-segment 120 prov120
tip: Give a use case for each: provider for direct addressing, tenant for self-service isolation.

q: How do VXLAN and Geneve overlays work, and what is the MTU consequence?
a: An overlay wraps each guest Ethernet frame inside a UDP packet that travels over the underlay between hypervisors. VXLAN uses a 24-bit virtual network identifier, so you can have about sixteen million segments instead of 4094 VLANs, with UDP port 4789. Geneve is the more extensible successor used by OVN, with variable-length options that carry metadata such as logical port identifiers. The cost is overhead: VXLAN adds about 50 bytes, Geneve about 58 or more, so if the underlay MTU is 1500 the guest MTU must be lowered to about 1442, otherwise large packets are fragmented or dropped, and you see the classic symptom of small requests working while large transfers hang. The fix is either a larger underlay MTU, such as 9000 jumbo frames, or advertising the correct smaller MTU to instances through DHCP.
f: How would you detect an MTU mismatch?
Why jumbo frames on the underlay?
p: Overlays encapsulate guest frames in UDP between hypervisors, adding 50 to 58 bytes of header. Raise the underlay MTU or lower the guest MTU, or large packets will hang.
tip: The symptom-based answer: small packets work, big ones hang.

q: What is DVR and when is it useful with OVS ML2?
a: Distributed Virtual Routing moves the L3 function from a few central network nodes onto every compute node. Without it, all routed traffic and all floating IP traffic hairpin through the network node, creating a bottleneck and single point of failure. With DVR, east-west traffic between subnets is routed locally on the compute node, and north-south traffic for instances with floating IPs goes directly out from the compute node through a floating IP namespace, while instances without floating IPs still use centralised SNAT on a network node. It improves scale and latency, but it adds complexity, more namespaces, more agents and harder debugging, and it requires external connectivity on compute nodes. With OVN this distributed behaviour is built in, so DVR is mainly a topic for ML2 OVS clouds.
f: Which traffic still goes through the network node?
How does OVN change this?
p: DVR runs routers on compute nodes so east-west and floating IP traffic avoid the network node bottleneck. Centralised SNAT remains for instances without floating IPs. OVN does this natively.
cmds: ip netns exec qrouter-<id> ip a
tip: Say what remains centralised, which shows depth.

q: How do floating IPs and SNAT work for instances?
a: A private instance sends traffic to its subnet gateway, which is a Neutron router. For outbound traffic without a floating IP, the router performs source NAT, replacing the instance address with the router's external gateway address, so many instances share one public IP. A floating IP is a one-to-one NAT mapping: Neutron associates a public address from an external network pool with the instance port, and the router performs DNAT for inbound traffic and SNAT for outbound traffic using that address. The instance itself never sees the public address, only its private one. Security groups still apply to the private port, so you must allow inbound traffic there. For troubleshooting I check the router namespace NAT rules, the external gateway, the instance security group, and whether the upstream network knows how to reach the floating range, often through ARP or BGP.
f: Why do floating IPs fail even when the association exists?
How is the floating pool routed upstream?
p: Routers SNAT outbound traffic and floating IPs add one-to-one DNAT and SNAT. Instances keep private addresses and security groups apply to the private port.
cmds: openstack server add floating ip web1 203.0.113.10
ip netns exec qrouter-<id> iptables -t nat -S | grep 203.0.113.10
tip: Remember to say the upstream network must route the floating range.

q: How do security groups work and how are they implemented?
a: A security group is a set of stateful allow rules attached to a port. By default all inbound traffic is denied and all outbound is allowed, and you add rules by direction, protocol, port range, and either a CIDR or another security group as the source, which is very useful for tier-to-tier rules such as allowing the app group to reach the database group. Because they are stateful, return traffic is permitted automatically through connection tracking. In ML2 OVS, rules become iptables or OVS flows with conntrack on the compute host, in the native OVS firewall driver, and in OVN they are ACLs translated into logical flows. Port security also adds anti-spoofing, preventing a guest from sending packets with another MAC or IP address. For debugging, I check the rules, the attached groups on the port, and the conntrack entries on the host.
f: Why reference a security group as a source?
How do you disable port security for an NFV instance?
p: Stateful allow-only rules attached to ports, with default deny inbound. Implemented as conntrack-based OVS flows or OVN ACLs; port security blocks spoofing.
cmds: openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-group app-sg db-sg
tip: Mention group-to-group rules, which scale better than CIDR lists.

q: What is Octavia and how does it provide load balancing as a service?
a: Octavia is the load-balancing service for OpenStack. When a user creates a load balancer, a listener, a pool and members, the Octavia controller builds an amphora, which is a small virtual machine running HAProxy and keepalived, in a management network, and configures it through a REST agent. In active-standby topology two amphorae share a virtual IP using VRRP, so a failure of one is handled automatically. Octavia supports L4 and L7 policies, TLS termination with certificates stored in Barbican, health monitors, and since newer releases, a provider framework with OVN as a lightweight L4 provider that avoids amphora VMs. For Kubernetes on OpenStack, the cloud provider uses Octavia to create service type LoadBalancer. Operationally I watch amphora health, image updates, the management network, and quota for the load balancer project.
f: What is an amphora?
When would you use the OVN provider instead?
p: Octavia creates HAProxy-based amphora VMs, optionally in active-standby with VRRP, and offers L4/L7, TLS termination and health monitors. The OVN provider is a lightweight L4 option.
cmds: openstack loadbalancer listener create --protocol HTTPS --protocol-port 443 lb1
tip: Link Octavia to Kubernetes services of type LoadBalancer.

q: An instance does not get an IP address from DHCP. How do you troubleshoot?
a: I work from the guest outward. First I check the instance console log to see whether the DHCP client ran and what it sent. Second, I confirm the port is ACTIVE and bound to the expected host, because a port in DOWN or binding failed means the data plane is not wired. Third, I verify the DHCP agent or OVN DHCP is alive for that network, that the subnet has DHCP enabled and free addresses, and that the port's MAC and IP are registered. Fourth, I capture traffic on the tap interface, the integration bridge and the dnsmasq namespace, looking for the DISCOVER and OFFER. Common causes are security group rules or port security blocking, an overlay MTU problem, a down agent, an exhausted subnet, or a mismatched VLAN on a provider network. I fix the specific layer and retest.
f: How do you capture on a tap device?
What if only some instances fail?
p: Check console log, port status and binding, DHCP agent and subnet state, then capture DISCOVER/OFFER on tap, bridge and namespace. Usual culprits: agent down, binding failure, MTU, VLAN, exhausted pool.
cmds: ip netns exec qdhcp-<net> tcpdump -ni any port 67 or port 68
tip: Narrate layer by layer: guest, port, agent, wire.

q: What does a Neutron port binding failure mean and how do you fix it?
a: When an instance boots, Nova asks Neutron to bind the port to the chosen host. Neutron's ML2 asks each mechanism driver whether it can bind that port on that host for a network of that type. If none can, the port ends in binding_failed, and the instance goes to ERROR. Typical causes are an agent that is down or not reporting on that host, a missing or misnamed physical network mapping such as bridge_mappings, a network type that the host does not support, or a mechanism driver misconfiguration, for example an SR-IOV request on a host without VFs. I read the port's binding profile and vif_type, check agent status on the host, compare the physnet name with the host configuration, and look at the neutron-server log for the reason. After fixing the cause, I rebuild or recreate the instance.
f: Where is physical network mapping configured?
How can the host agent list help?
p: Binding fails when no mechanism driver can bind the port on that host: agent down, wrong physnet mapping or unsupported network type. Inspect vif_type, agent state and server logs.
tip: Say vif_type=binding_failed and then check agent, physnet, type.

q: How do you debug network paths using namespaces, tcpdump and flows?
a: I follow the packet through each hop. On the compute host the path is guest, tap or vhost-user device, integration bridge br-int, then the tunnel bridge or provider bridge, and out to the physical NIC. I start with ip link and bridge checks, then use tcpdump on the tap and on the physical interface to see where packets stop. For routers and DHCP in ML2 OVS, I enter the network namespace with ip netns exec and run ip, iptables and tcpdump inside it. For flow-level problems, I use ovs-ofctl dump-flows and ovs-appctl ofproto/trace to simulate a packet and show which rule matches. With OVN, ovn-trace does the same for logical flows. Comparing where a packet is seen last tells me which component is dropping it.
f: What does ofproto/trace give you?
How do you capture on a vhost-user interface?
p: Trace hop by hop: tap, br-int, tunnel or provider bridge, NIC. Use ip netns exec for routers and DHCP, and ovs-appctl ofproto/trace or ovn-trace to find the dropping rule.
cmds: ip netns exec qrouter-<id> tcpdump -ni any icmp
tip: The last hop where you still see the packet is where it gets dropped.

q: What is SR-IOV and how do you use it with OpenStack?
a: SR-IOV lets a physical NIC present multiple virtual functions, each a lightweight PCIe device that can be assigned directly to a guest, bypassing the host's virtual switch. This gives near line rate throughput and low latency with little CPU use, which suits NFV, telco and high-throughput workloads. In OpenStack you enable VFs on the NIC and IOMMU in the BIOS and kernel, whitelist the physical network in the Nova PCI configuration, enable the sriovnicswitch mechanism driver in Neutron with the SR-IOV agent, and create ports with vnic_type direct. The trade-offs are significant: no software security groups on the data path in many setups, limited live migration support, hardware-specific drivers in the guest, and fewer overlay features. I use it where performance justifies those constraints, and keep a normal OVS path for everything else.
f: Why is live migration hard with SR-IOV?
What replaces security groups here?
p: SR-IOV assigns NIC virtual functions straight to guests for near line-rate networking. Use vnic_type direct, whitelist in Nova, and accept limits on migration and software filtering.
cmds: openstack port create --vnic-type direct --network sriov-net sriov-port
tip: State the trade-off: speed versus features such as migration and filtering.

q: How does Neutron QoS work and what can it limit?
a: The QoS extension lets you define policies with rules and attach them to ports or networks. Supported rule types include bandwidth limit, which caps egress or ingress rate, minimum bandwidth, which guarantees capacity and is enforced through Placement so the scheduler considers it, DSCP marking to set packet priority, and packet rate limits. The back end enforces it: OVS uses ingress policing and queues, OVN uses meters and QoS tables, and SR-IOV applies limits on the virtual function. I use QoS to stop one tenant saturating an uplink, to provide tiered network service levels, and to protect latency-sensitive traffic with DSCP. The limitations are that enforcement depends on the driver, that ingress and egress behave differently, and that without a minimum bandwidth guarantee QoS only restricts but does not promise capacity.
f: How does minimum bandwidth interact with Placement?
Which direction is easier to limit?
p: QoS policies attach bandwidth, minimum bandwidth, DSCP and packet-rate rules to ports or networks. Enforcement depends on the driver, and minimum guarantees need Placement support.
cmds: openstack network qos policy create gold
openstack network qos rule create --type bandwidth-limit --max-kbps 100000 --egress gold

q: What are trunk ports and when are they needed?
a: A trunk port carries traffic for several VLANs over a single virtual NIC. The parent port belongs to one network, and subports are attached with VLAN IDs, so the guest sees tagged frames and can create VLAN subinterfaces for each. This is needed for workloads that expect to be multi-homed through VLANs, such as NFV appliances, virtual routers and firewalls, and for Kubernetes or container platforms running inside a VM where pods get their own Neutron networks, as with Kuryr. It saves you from hot-plugging many separate ports, which hit hypervisor PCI slot limits. Operationally, you create the parent port, add subports with segmentation type vlan and ID, and in the guest configure matching VLAN interfaces. I verify tags at the bridge level if packets are missing.
f: How does the guest need to be configured?
Why not just add many NICs?
p: A trunk carries multiple tagged VLANs on one vNIC via a parent port and subports. Used by NFV appliances and nested container networking to avoid many NICs.
cmds: openstack network trunk create --parent-port p0 trunk0
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.101 type vlan id 101
tip: Mention Kuryr or NFV as the real-world use.

q: How do you handle IPv6 and dual stack in OpenStack?
a: Neutron supports IPv6 subnets with either SLAAC, DHCPv6 stateless or stateful modes, controlled by ipv6_ra_mode and ipv6_address_mode. Router advertisements are generated by the router or the OVN logical router so guests configure addresses automatically. For dual stack, a network has both an IPv4 and an IPv6 subnet and ports receive both. There is no NAT for IPv6 by default, so instances get globally routable addresses, which means security groups become the primary protection, and the upstream network must route the prefix, either through static routes or BGP dynamic routing and prefix delegation. Common problems are forgetting IPv6 rules in security groups, an upstream that does not route the tenant prefix, and images that do not run an IPv6 client. I test with ping6 and a real application, not only router advertisements.
f: Why do security groups matter more for IPv6?
What does prefix delegation provide?
p: IPv6 uses SLAAC or DHCPv6 with router advertisements. Dual stack gives both address families; there is no NAT, so security groups and upstream routing of the prefix are essential.
cmds: openstack subnet create --ip-version 6 --ipv6-ra-mode slaac --ipv6-address-mode slaac --network n1 --subnet-range 2001:db8:1::/64 v6
openstack security group rule create --ethertype IPv6 --protocol icmpv6 default
tip: Point out that no NAT shifts protection to security groups.

q: How does Neutron integrate with BGP and dynamic routing?
a: For public address space, the upstream needs to know where tenant or floating prefixes live. Neutron dynamic routing provides a BGP speaker that advertises tenant subnets and floating IPs to physical routers, so you do not maintain static routes. It uses address scopes and subnet pools to make sure only the right prefixes are advertised. With OVN, a BGP agent for OVN or an integration with FRR can advertise routes directly from each compute host, enabling routed networks where each rack is its own L3 domain, which avoids large stretched L2 segments and gives better scalability and failure isolation. I use this in leaf-spine fabrics: addresses are announced from where they live, ECMP gives load balancing, and failure convergence is handled by the routing protocol instead of VRRP or ARP tricks.
f: What are address scopes for?
Why prefer routed networks over stretched L2?
p: Neutron BGP speakers or OVN with FRR advertise tenant and floating prefixes to the fabric, enabling routed leaf-spine designs without stretched L2 or static routes.
tip: Say leaf-spine with ECMP and per-rack L3 domains.

q: What are Designate and DNS integration in Neutron?
a: Designate is the DNS as a service project. Users create zones and recordsets through an API, and Designate publishes them to authoritative servers such as BIND or PowerDNS through a pool configuration. Neutron integrates with it so that when a port or floating IP is created, a DNS record is created automatically, for example web1.example.org pointing to the instance address, using the dns_name and dns_domain attributes, and removed again on deletion. This avoids manual DNS and stale records, and provides internal names for instances in a project. For internal resolution inside a tenant, Neutron DHCP can also serve DNS through dnsmasq with a configured forwarder. In production I decide who owns each zone, keep tenant zones separate from platform zones, and monitor propagation and the sink service that listens to notifications.
f: What is the Designate sink?
How do you keep tenants from creating records in platform zones?
p: Designate offers DNS as a service publishing to BIND or PowerDNS. Neutron integration creates and removes records for ports and floating IPs automatically.
tip: Mention zone ownership and delegation for tenants.

q: How do you design the physical network for an OpenStack cloud?
a: I separate traffic types, usually into management, API, tunnel or overlay, storage, and external or provider networks, either as separate VLANs on bonded NICs or on separate physical interfaces. Storage traffic, especially Ceph, gets its own high-bandwidth and ideally non-oversubscribed path, with a separate replication network. The overlay network needs a larger MTU. Each node has redundant NICs in LACP or active-backup bonds connected to two top-of-rack switches in MLAG or a leaf-spine fabric with ECMP. The control plane sits on a stable L2 or L3 segment with a virtual IP managed by keepalived. I plan IP address ranges, VLAN ranges, firewalling between planes, and capacity with oversubscription ratios. Documenting the design as a diagram and an addressing table is as important as the hardware, because troubleshooting depends on it.
f: Why separate storage and tenant traffic?
What bonding mode would you use?
p: Separate management, API, overlay, storage and provider traffic; bond NICs across two ToR switches; jumbo MTU for overlay and storage; plan IPs and VLANs and document them.
tip: Lead with traffic separation, then redundancy, then MTU.

q: What is the metadata proxy path and why do some instances fail to get SSH keys?
a: Instances request metadata from 169.254.169.254. In ML2 OVS the request reaches a metadata proxy running in the router or DHCP namespace, which adds the instance and network identity and forwards it over a Unix socket to the neutron-metadata-agent, then to the Nova metadata API with a shared secret signature. In OVN the ovn-metadata-agent on each host serves this through a namespace and haproxy. Failures leave cloud-init with no key or user data. Causes include a missing route or DHCP option for the link-local address, the metadata agent being down, a shared secret mismatch between Neutron and Nova, a security group blocking egress to the address, or the Nova metadata API being unreachable. I curl the endpoint from inside the guest through a console, then walk the chain, agent, secret, Nova API.
f: What is the shared secret for?
How does a config drive avoid all this?
p: 169.254.169.254 requests go through a namespace proxy and the metadata agent to Nova metadata, signed with a shared secret. Failures: agent down, secret mismatch, routing or egress blocked.
tip: Name the shared-secret mismatch, a classic cause.
